```{r, include = FALSE}
has_suggests <- all(vapply(c("ggplot2", "tidyr", "patchwork"),
  requireNamespace, logical(1),
  quietly = TRUE
))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#",
  eval = has_suggests,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 7,
  fig.dpi = 300,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(varunayan)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)
```

`get_era5_country_temperature()` does three steps.
First, the function finds the boundary of a country.
Then it downloads monthly ERA5 data.
Then it returns national averages with cosine-latitude area weights.

One call does all of these steps.
You do not have to find boundaries, write GeoJSON, call `era5ify_geojson()`, and aggregate grid cells manually.

In this example, we get the monthly mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures for 2024.
We get these data for four European countries and four South Asian countries.

## Download data

We give the short values `"mean"`, `"max"`, and `"min"` to the `variables` argument.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
countries <- c(
  "France", "Germany", "Spain", "Norway",
  "India", "Pakistan", "Bangladesh", "Nepal"
)

all_data <- lapply(countries, function(cntry) {
  df <- get_era5_country_temperature(
    country    = cntry,
    start_date = "2024-01-01",
    end_date   = "2024-12-31",
    variables  = c("mean", "max", "min")
  )
  df$country <- cntry
  df
})

temps <- bind_rows(all_data)
```

```{r load-data, echo = FALSE}
temps <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "country_temps.rds", package = "varunayan"))
```

```{r preview}
head(temps)
```

We add the region of each country to the data.
The plots use the region to make facets.

```{r regions}
region_map <- c(
  France = "Europe", Germany = "Europe", Spain = "Europe", Norway = "Europe",
  India = "South Asia", Pakistan = "South Asia",
  Bangladesh = "South Asia", Nepal = "South Asia"
)

temps$region <- region_map[temps$country]
temps$month_label <- factor(month.abb[temps$month], levels = month.abb)

# Cool colors for Europe, warm colors for South Asia
country_colors <- c(
  France = "#2166AC", Germany = "#4393C3",
  Spain = "#92C5DE", Norway = "#053061",
  India = "#B2182B", Pakistan = "#D6604D",
  Bangladesh = "#F4A582", Nepal = "#67001F"
)
```

## Seasonal heatmap

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(temps, aes(x = month_label, y = country, fill = temperature_mean)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(region ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "RdYlBu", direction = -1,
    name = "Mean temp (\u00B0C)"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    title = "Mean monthly temperature by country (2024)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold")
  )
```

The temperatures of South Asian countries stay more than 20 &deg;C for all of the year.
The temperatures of European countries change by more than 20 &deg;C between winter and summer.
In Norway, the temperature is less than 0 &deg;C from November to March.

## Monthly trend lines with min/max ribbon

```{r trendlines, fig.height = 8}
ggplot(temps, aes(x = month, color = country, fill = country)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = temperature_min, ymax = temperature_max),
    alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temperature_mean), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = temperature_mean), size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Temperature (\u00B0C)",
    title = "Monthly temperature with min-max range (2024)",
    subtitle = "Ribbon: national-average daily min to daily max",
    color = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Diurnal range

The diurnal temperature range (DTR) is the difference between the daily maximum and the daily minimum.
The DTR is larger in continental and arid climates than in humid tropical climates.

```{r dtr, fig.height = 6}
temps$dtr <- temps$temperature_max - temps$temperature_min

ggplot(temps, aes(x = month, y = dtr, color = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Diurnal temperature range (\u00B0C)",
    title = "Monthly diurnal temperature range (2024)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Regional comparison

Last, we show all eight countries on one axis.
The line type shows the region of each country.

```{r comparison, fig.height = 6}
ggplot(temps, aes(
  x = month, y = temperature_mean,
  color = country, linetype = region
)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Europe" = "solid", "South Asia" = "dashed")) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Mean temperature (\u00B0C)",
    title = "Europe vs South Asia: monthly temperature (2024)",
    color = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
